### Question 1

MRI uses a giant, super-strong magnet and radio waves to take pictures of the inside of your body without cutting it open. The 'M' is for Magnetic, the 'R' is for Resonance (how the magnet makes tiny parts of you signal back), and the 'I' is for Imaging (making a picture). So when you read MRI, think 'magnet camera.'

### Question 2

A CBC is like taking a headcount of everything floating in your blood: the red cells that carry oxygen, the white cells that fight germs, and the platelets that help you stop bleeding. 'Complete' means it counts all the main players, and 'Count' means it literally tallies them up. Think of it as a roll call for your blood.

### Question 3

When your heart pumps, it pushes blood through your arteries like water pushing through a garden hose. BP measures how hard that blood is pushing on the walls of the hose. 'B' is Blood and 'P' is Pressure, so BP is just how strongly your blood is pressing.

### Question 4

Both make slice-by-slice pictures of your insides, but they use different 'flashlights.' CT uses X-rays, the same kind of energy as a regular X-ray photo, so it uses radiation. MRI uses a big magnet and radio waves instead, so no radiation. Same goal (pictures in slices), different tools.

### Question 5

Sometimes the same thing has two nicknames because it came from two languages. In English 'cardio' starts with a C, but in German it starts with a K ('Kardio'). So ECG and EKG are two spellings of the exact same heart test that records the heart's electrical signals. Same test, two nicknames.

### Question 6

When you give medicine, it matters HOW it gets in: swallowed (PO, 'by mouth'), into a vein (IV), or into a muscle (IM). These short codes are like delivery instructions on a package telling you which door to use. They don't tell you how much to give, what legal class the drug is in, or when the vial expires; they tell you the way it goes in.

### Question 7

Some shortcuts look too much like numbers. A quick 'U' for units can look like a 0, so '4U' might be read as '40', which could be ten times too much medicine. Writing out the whole word 'units' fixes the confusion. Clear writing beats fast writing when someone's safety is on the line.

### Question 8

NPO is a Latin shortcut for 'nothing by mouth.' If a sign said NPO after midnight, it means no snacks, no water, nothing to swallow once the clock hits twelve, usually so the stomach is empty for a test or surgery. Think of it as a 'kitchen closed' sign for that patient.

### Question 9

Your kidneys are like a filter that cleans waste out of your blood. BUN and Cr are two kinds of waste. If the filter is working well, only a little is left in the blood; if a lot piles up, the filter (kidney) might be struggling. So doctors check BUN and Cr to see how well the kidneys are cleaning.

### Question 10

SOB means 'shortness of breath', when someone feels like they can't get enough air. SpO2 measures how much oxygen is actually riding in the blood, usually with a little clip on the finger. So the note is saying: the person felt out of breath, so we checked whether their blood was getting enough oxygen. One follows naturally from the other.

### Question 11

This order is like a recipe made of shortcuts. 'mg' is the amount (milligrams), 'PO' means swallow it, and 'BID' is Latin shorthand ('bis in die') for two times each day. Put the pieces together and it says: swallow 40 milligrams, twice a day. If you mix up BID with something else, the patient gets the wrong number of doses.

### Question 12

'q.d.' is supposed to mean once a day, but if the handwriting is messy it can look like 'q.i.d.', which means four times a day, four times too much medicine. Because those two look-alikes are so easy to mix up, the safe move is to just write the plain word 'daily.' Clear words beat risky shortcuts.
